### A B-tree index improves lookup efficiency through a hierarchical tree structure

A B-tree index speeds up lookups by turning a scan of the whole table into a short walk down a tree.

### How a B-tree index executes lookups and supports operations

Without an index, finding a row by some column means reading every row (a full table scan), which is O(n). 

A B-tree keeps the indexed values in sorted order, organized as a shallow, wide tree:

Each node is sized to fit a disk page (commonly 4-16 KB) and holds hundreds of keys, each with a pointer to a child node.

A lookup proceeds through the following steps:
1. A lookup starts at the root.
2. Binary-searches the keys in that node to pick the right child.
3. Repeats until it reaches a leaf. 
4. The leaf holds the key and a pointer to the actual row (or, in a clustered index, the row itself).

Because each node has such a high fan-out, the tree stays very shallow. 

With ~500 keys per node, three levels address about 125 million entries and four levels address about 60 billion. 

So a lookup costs O(log n) page reads, usually 3-4, and the top levels are almost always cached in memory, so often only one or two reads actually hit disk.

Sorted order also helps beyond exact matches. Range queries (BETWEEN, >, <), ORDER BY, prefix matches (LIKE 'abc%'), and min/max can all walk adjacent leaves, which in most implementations (B+trees) are linked together.

```diagram
Root node -> Child node: binary-search keys for child pointer
Child node -> Leaf node: repeat traversal to leaf
Leaf node -> Row: access key and pointer to row (or row itself)
```

### The performance and resource costs introduced by B-tree indexes

Slower writes. Every INSERT and DELETE must update each index on the table, and an UPDATE to an indexed column must remove and re-insert the entry. Each index adds extra page writes plus write-ahead log traffic.

Page splits and fragmentation. When a node fills up, it splits, which costs extra I/O. Random keys (like UUIDv4) scatter inserts across the tree and cause more splits and cache misses than sequential keys. Over time, deletes and splits leave pages partly empty, so indexes can bloat and need rebuilding or vacuuming.

Storage space. An index stores a copy of the indexed columns plus pointers. Wide or numerous indexes can rival or exceed the size of the table itself, and they compete with table data for buffer cache memory.

Maintenance and planning overhead. More indexes mean longer bulk loads, longer backups and rebuilds, and more choices for the query planner, which can occasionally pick a poor plan. Unused indexes pay all the write costs and give nothing back.

Limited usefulness in some cases. A B-tree doesn’t help when the query isn’t selective (if a filter matches 30% of the table, a sequential scan is often faster), when a function is applied to the column (WHERE lower(name) = ... without a matching expression index), or when a composite index is queried without its leading column.

Rule of thumb: indexes trade write speed and space for read speed, so they pay off on columns that are frequently filtered, joined, or sorted on and are reasonably selective, and they hurt on write-heavy tables with many rarely used indexes.

primary_claims: A B-tree index reduces lookup complexity from O(n) full table scan to O(log n) tree traversal.
High fan-out and shallow tree depth result in 3 to 4 page reads for millions or billions of entries.
B-tree indexes support range queries, order by, and prefix matches via linked leaves.
Indexes impose costs including slower writes, page splits, fragmentation, storage space, and maintenance overhead.
B-tree indexes are ineffective for non-selective queries, functions on columns, or queries missing leading composite index columns.

assumed_prior_knowledge: Familiarity with relational database operations like INSERT, DELETE, UPDATE, and JOIN.
Understanding of the performance difference between reading from disk versus reading from memory cache.
possible_confusions: Confusing non-clustered indexes with clustered indexes regarding whether the leaf points to a row pointer or the actual row data.
ambiguous_references: which in most implementations (B+trees) are linked together (refers to adjacent leaves)

learning_objectives: Understand how B-tree indexes convert O(n) table scans into O(log n) tree traversals
Explain how high fan-out and shallow tree depth minimize disk page reads
Identify the trade-offs and performance costs associated with B-tree indexes, including write overhead, fragmentation, and storage
explanation_sequence: Contrast full table scans O(n) with B-tree index lookups O(log n)
Explain B-tree structure including nodes, disk pages, keys, and pointers
Describe how high fan-out results in a shallow tree requiring only 3-4 page reads
Explain how sorted leaves support range queries and order by operations
Detail the costs of indexes including slower writes, page splits, storage space, and maintenance overhead
Discuss limitations such as non-selective queries and missing leading composite index columns
plan.analogy_rationale: An analogy comparing a B-tree index to a book index or a corporate directory helps visualize how navigating a hierarchical structure avoids reading every single page.

preserved_claims: A B-tree keeps keys in sorted order so the database can narrow down to a row instead of scanning every row.
Each step down the tree removes a large share of the remaining rows, so lookups take roughly logarithmic time.
The index must be updated on every insert, update, and delete, which makes writes slower.
The index takes up extra storage space in addition to the table itself.
